title: Concession temperament and scriptlets
content:
Purpose: quick personal cheat-sheet for fast redlines and on-call negotiation instincts. Put next to laptop during customer calls. Not canonical legal language — use as prompt for LGL review.

Top-level posture (short):
- Goal: keep customer comfort (no blocking commitments) while preserving Redwood’s product flexibility and bounded liability.
- Tone: collaborative, pragmatic, avoid categorical "never"s unless safety/regulatory.

Clauses to triage immediately (severity buckets and quick stances):
1) Indemnity / third-party claims (High)
   - Red flags: uncapped indemnity, IP indemnity for model outputs, indemnity for customer data that includes model behavior claims.
   - Quick stance: offer mutual indemnity for direct IP infringement claims, carve out "model outputs" from customer-IP indemnity or limited to willful misuse. Cap indemnity at a multiple of fees (typically 1x-3x) — recommend 1x for hosted, 3x only for enterprise with dedicated capacity and significant MRR.
   - Scriptlets: "We can do mutual indemnity for direct infringement claims tied to content customers supply. For model outputs we need a narrow, usage-based carve-out — can you share a specific risk example?"

2) Liability cap & consequential damages (High)
   - Red flags: unlimited liability, broad carve-out of consequential damages in customer favor, aggregator of downstream losses.
   - Quick stance: liability cap = greater of fees paid in prior 12 months or $1M (scale by deal size). Always exclude gross negligence and willful misconduct from cap conversation but avoid making them carve-outs that swallow the cap. Carve out regulatory fines carefully.
   - Scriptlets: "We’re happy to put a commercial cap aligned to the last-12-months of fees. For regulatory fines, let’s map to specific obligations — can you point to an example you're concerned about?"

3) Data residency & export controls (Medium-High)
   - Red flags: customer demands strict geographic residency for logs + model artifacts + backups + KV caches; blanket prohibition on export; airtight deletion guarantees without a roadmap.
   - Quick stance: we can commit to region for customer data at rest and to reasonable operational controls for caches; model checkpoints and curated internal artifacts cannot be guaranteed to never leave region unless Private on-prem/VPC. Offer Private or Dedicated for true residency needs.
   - Scriptlets: "For strict residency, our Private deployment is the right fit. For hosted plans we can narrow log routing and retention windows — what is the minimum residency requirement you need?"

4) Model output IP & ownership (High)
   - Red flags: customer claiming exclusive ownership of all outputs, assignment of underlying model rights, or broad license-back of Redwood tech.
   - Quick stance: Customer gets a license to use outputs for their internal and customer-facing purposes; Redwood retains rights in models and improvements. If customer needs exclusivity, treat as a premium feature (dedicated model instance + contract term + higher fees).
   - Scriptlets: "Outputs: you get a right to use and sublicense outputs you generate. We can discuss exclusivity for an additional commitment — can you quantify exclusivity scope/duration?"

5) Audit & access / security assessments (Medium)
   - Red flags: on-site audits, unfettered code access, or root credential requests.
   - Quick stance: provide SOC reports, pen test summaries, and a reasonable remote audit process. On-site or source-code review only for Private/on-prem — otherwise provide redacted logs and a security questionnaire.
   - Scriptlets: "We can provide our latest SOC2 report and a security questionnaire; for source-level access we'd need a Private deployment and an NDA scope — is that what you had in mind?"

6) Subprocessors & third-party risk (Medium)
   - Red flags: customer wants pre-approval for every subprocessor; requires right to veto vendors.
   - Quick stance: maintain a published subprocessor list, give 30 days notice and allow contract-level remedies rather than wholesale veto. For specific high-risk vendors (KMS/HSM, model hosting partners), escalate to SRE/security for mitigation language.
   - Scriptlets: "We publish our subprocessor list and will provide notice prior to changes. For KMS/HSM we can discuss separate controls or on-prem integrations."

7) Termination & transition assistance (Medium)
   - Red flags: indefinite transition assistance at no cost, excessive data export obligations beyond stored data, live-run support obligations.
   - Quick stance: provide 90 days of assistance and data export in customer format; additional professional services billed. For enterprise, negotiated transition plan with fees.
   - Scriptlets: "Standard exit support is 90 days with data export. If you need extended runout or help rehosting, we can quote professional services."

Negotiation posture & concession ladder (personal shorthand):
- Tier 1 (quick trade): swap for something low-cost operationally (e.g., longer invoicing window, slightly longer retention, non-material SLA tweak).
- Tier 2 (product upgrade): propose Dedicated/Private or add-on (SLA/retention/region) for elevated asks.
- Tier 3 (commercial): accept larger exposure only with increased fees, indemnity cap increases tied to premium, and stronger insurance requirements.

Insurance & financial hygiene (notes):
- Standard ask: general liability + tech E&O; Minimum $1M each, $2M preferred for enterprise.
- If indemnity cap > $5M push for $5M E&O and evidence of coverage.

Specific language brushes (templates to paste quickly):
- Limited outputs license: "Provider grants Customer a non-exclusive, worldwide, royalty-free license to use, reproduce, modify, and distribute Outputs generated by Customer's use of the Service solely for Customer’s internal business purposes and to provide services to its end users."
- Indemnity cap suggestion: "Provider's aggregate liability shall not exceed the greater of (a) the fees paid by Customer under the Order Form in the 12 months preceding the claim, or (b) $1,000,000."
- Data residency fallback: "Provider will, where Customer purchases a region-specific deployment, ensure Customer Data at rest is stored in the selected region except for transient caching necessary for low-latency operation."

Escalation triggers (who to pull in):
- Security escalation: immediate if customer requests source access, HSM details, or vendor veto — pull Rina Koh (Security) + SRE lead.
- Commercial escalation: if customer demands uncapped liability or unlimited indemnity — pull Diego (Sales Ops) + CFO rep.
- Legal nuance escalation: IP ownership or exclusivity ask — loop in outside counsel + LGL lead.

Open questions / TODOs (for LGL sync):
- Define exact indemnity carve-outs for model outputs (need precedent language).
- Agree on standard numeric caps by product tier (hosted vs dedicated vs private).
- Finalize phrasing for transient cache/residency exception.

Notes to self:
- Keep scripts short and open-ended; avoid binary refutations. Ask customers for examples and use-cases — that buys time.
- Offer product alternatives (dedicated/private) early if ask is heavy on residency/IP.
- For in-person exec meetings, prepare 1-pager on "what exclusivity means technically" and commercial tradeoffs.

Recent quick wins (copyable proofs):
- "We change raw log retention to 30 days and provide S3 export on request — customer accepted."
- "Moved liability cap from unlimited to fees-in-last-12-months + $1M floor — closed after premium fee add-on."

Anchors to watch (bad signs):
- Customer asks for both exclusivity and zero-fee.
- Repeated requests for source access without comms on what they actually need.
- Sliding timeframe demands for deletion without log/backup carve-outs.

References (internal):
- Confluence: Licensing and IP norms (CONFLUENCE-1234-licensing-guidance)
- Jira: Legal precedents and redlines (JIRA-LEGAL-88)

End — keep updating as we see more patterns.

— A.P.
